Instructions: For each paper (each row), the labeling process would follow these steps:
2. Based on the paper's title, abstract, and full text, does any benchmark the paper proposes evaluate tool-use LLM agents?
label: yes
definition: At least one proposed benchmark evaluates LLM agents that call tools (e.g. bash shell, MCP), including coding agents. Judge the benchmark itself (its tasks and the models evaluated on it), not the methods or baselines the paper proposes to solve its tasks. It counts if the evaluated models write code that is executed (coding agents generally count), call tools, functions, or APIs (whether the calls run live or are scored against expected calls), or operate a computer, browser, or mobile device through GUI actions executed in an environment. It does not count if the models only write text, only pick from a fixed menu of moves or make decisions in a simulation, only judge recorded agent trajectories, or never call tools; tool-using agents used only to evaluate the models do not count either. Take as given that the paper proposes a benchmark

Instructions: 3. Based on the paper's title, abstract, and full text, does any benchmark the paper proposes have a safety/security focus?
label: yes
definition: At least one proposed benchmark evaluates, as its focus or as a substantial part (such as a dedicated evaluation axis, dimension, or category), something agent users, developers, or affected parties would want to prevent: harm to people, privacy, systems, or data caused by the agent, or the agent breaking safety, security, or domain policies it is given in its prompts or tool descriptions, including conditions a tool states must hold before use. Benchmarks where agents perform security tasks or show dangerous capabilities also count; step 4 excludes them. Ordinary task-quality failures (incorrect, low-quality, or hallucinated outputs) count only if the paper frames them as a safety or security concern. Passing mentions or a token number of items do not count

Instructions: 4. Based on the paper's title, abstract, and full text, is the paper out of scope? Judge by what the benchmark measures, not by its topic.
label: yes
definition:
("why out of scope": perform security/safety tasks)
The benchmark measures how well an agent performs security- or safety-related tasks (e.g. patch code vulnerabilities), not whether the agent itself behaves safely/securely

label: yes
definition:
("why out of scope": duplicated)
This paper extends another benchmark/dataset that is included in another paper labeled earlier, while this paper adds only data or metrics to the benchmark/dataset without changing security or safety policies, or that the policies is changed only in languages (e.g. English to Spanish). Please add a note which earlier paper this duplicates

label: yes
definition:
("why out of scope": threat)
The benchmark tests whether an agent could pose a threat: whether it can plausibly achieve a dangerous behavior, or whether it will carry the behavior out when told to. Benchmarks that test whether an agent refuses or complies with harmful user requests measure safe behavior and are in scope

label: no
definition: Otherwise; leave "why out of scope" blank

Instructions: 5. Based on the paper's title, abstract, and full text, does the benchmark target domain-specific or general-purpose agents?
label: domain-specific
definition: Both the instructions and the tools given to the agent are built for a specific domain. Coding and using a computer, browser, or phone are not specific domains. A generic instruction such as "assist the user" does not make the agent domain-specific, even if the tasks or environments it is tested on come from specific domains

Instructions: 6. Based on the paper's title, abstract, and full text, and optionally the codebase, is a safety/security policy given to the evaluated agent, and how verifiable is it? A policy is a natural-language instruction in the evaluated agent's system prompt, user prompt, or tool descriptions about whether or how to behave safely or securely, including conditions a tool states must hold before use. It counts even if the benchmark is designed to pressure or tempt the agent into breaking it. A safety prompt that the paper tests as a defense or mitigation counts only if its text is shown and the benchmark grades the same behavior it asks for. Not policies: structural defenses (delimiters, filters, detectors), automatically generated rules, hints about the specific flaw being tested, an instruction to make the output secure when the security of that output is what the benchmark measures, content the agent encounters in its environment, attack or test-scenario text, role or job descriptions, and rubrics given only to an evaluator.
label: N/A
definition: No policy is given to the evaluated agent, including when the only safety prompts are tested defenses that do not count (for example, because their text is not shown)

label: Goal-Setting
definition: One policy applies across tasks, and it is not entirely checkable: it consists of high-level goals whose satisfaction cannot be verified from the agent's actions, possibly alongside a few concrete rules or prohibitions. A clearly stated rule that relies on an undefined concept (such as what counts as private, confidential, sensitive, or harmful) is a high-level goal

label: Verifiable-Rule
definition: One policy applies across tasks, and it is essentially a set of rules whose satisfaction can be verified from the agent's actions, with key concepts precisely defined. Judge from the policy text the agent receives, not from how the benchmark checks it

label: Task-Specific
definition: A safety/security instruction written for an individual task (one policy per task). Ordinary task goals or requirements, safety mentioned in passing, and descriptions of the situation or its norms are not policies. Do not infer a task-level policy from a single example

label: Unclear
definition: The paper does not show or explain the policy in the benchmark's standard setup well enough to classify it: it says the agent receives safety instructions but does not show them, or it names rules or constraints without explaining what they mean. A defense prompt whose text is not shown does not make the label Unclear; it does not count, as above
